G-4801-CI-0202402616-000
IN THE COURT OF COMMON PLEAS LUCAS COUNTY, OHIO
EFILED LUCAS COUNTY 8/27/2024 2:57 PM COMMON PLEAS COURT BERNIE QUILTER, CLERK EFILE ID: 124665
C
YODER MACHINERY SALES COMPANY,
Plaintiff,
VS.
WATERFORD BANK, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION, et al.,
Defendants.
CASE NO. G-4801-CI-0202402616- 000
JUDGE JOSEPH V. MCNAMARA
PLAINTIFF'S MEMORANDUM IN
OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT
YODER BROTHERS MACHINERY
LTD.'S, TIMOTHY YODER'S,
RYAN YODER'S, AND KORY
YODER'S MOTION FOR PARTIAL
JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS
INTRODUCTION
Defendants' motion elides the straightforward basis for its denial. Plaintiff Yoder Machin- ery Sales Company ("Plaintiff" or "Yoder Machinery") is not a party to the settlement agreement. We know that Plaintiff is not a party to the settlement agreement because the agreement tells us who the parties are, right at the outset and again in the signature blocks: "Terral Yoder" and "Tim- othy Yoder." Not Plaintiff. That is the plain and unambiguous language of the agreement.
Nevertheless, without addressing the real issue and without even making an ambiguity ar- gument, Defendants ask the Court to find against the plain language of the agreement based on extrinsic evidence. What Defendants are asking the Court to do-disregard the plain language of an agreement-is an extremely difficult lift, even with a good ambiguity argument (which De- fendants do not have) and a developed record (which Defendants also do not have). And even if the Court determined that the settlement agreement is ambiguous, that would simply confirm that the Yoder Brothers Defendants' Rule 12 motion is improper-because courts cannot consider ex- trinsic evidence on a motion for judgment on the pleadings. The Court should deny the motion.
1

-
RELEVANT FACTS
Defendants' motion includes a "statement of material facts not in dispute." Defs.' Mot. at 5 (capitalization altered). But many of these assertions are quite disputed, particularly the atextual claim that Terry signed the settlement agreement in a representative capacity on behalf of Yoder Machinery. Id. at 6. For the Court's reference, Plaintiff includes the following relevant facts from the Court's prior decisions, including in the real-estate lawsuit which Terry and Tim's 2021 set- tlement agreement resolved.
I. After Tim Left the Family Business, Terry and Tim Settled a Lawsuit over the Purchase Price of Tim's Share of Real Estate that the Brothers Jointly Owned.
Terry and Tim Yoder are brothers who, until 2019, jointly owned and operated Plaintiff Yoder Machinery Sales Company: Opinion and Judgment Entry, Terral Yoder, et al. v. Timothy Yoder, No. G-4801-CI-0201904611-000 (Jan. 26, 2021) ("Jan. 2021 Op."), at 1. "In January 2019, Tim agreed to sell his 50% ownership in [Yoder Machinery]," which entailed "sell[ing] his 50% interest in the real property located at 1500 Holloway Road ('Holloway Property'), where [Yoder Machinery] had been, and continues to be, housed." Id. at 1-2. "The parties formalized their agree- ment regarding the sale of the Holloway Property by executing a Real Estate Purchase Agree- ment," which "set forth the manner in which the purchase price of the Holloway Property would 1 be calculated[.]" Id. at 2. The purchase agreement required the closing for the real-estate purchase to occur by April 3, 2019. Id.
1
Because of disputes over the purchase price of the real property, the closing did not take place by April 2019. Jan. 2021 Op. at 2. Specifically, the real estate purchase agreement identified three appraisers for the brothers' real property, and those appraisers submitted widely divergent valuations for the Holloway Property. Id. at 3. The William Fall Group appraisal was $2.6 million higher than the next highest appraisal. Id. In December 2019, Terry and Yoder Machinery filed a
2

complaint against Tim, on the grounds that (among other things), "the William Fall Group ap- praisal is invalid due to bad faith activity on the part of Tim that amounts to a breach of the [real estate purchase agreement] contract." Id.
The Court agreed with Terry that there was at least a genuine issue of material fact as to whether Tim had acted in bad faith. Jan. 2021 Op. at 7-9. First, the Court determined that "the evidence suggests that the appraiser for the William Fall Group failed to use the income capitali- zation approach, not based on his own professional judgment, but because his client, Tim, asked him not to[,]" thereby "arguably reducing [the appraisal's] accuracy." Id. at 7. Second, the Court found that "there is evidence to suggest that the William Fall Group appraiser failed to understand the true purpose for the appraisal due to Tim's deliberate withholding of pertinent information." Id. at 8. Third, the Court determined that there was "evidence in the record to suggest that Tim provided false information in order to inflate the William Fall Group appraisal value." Id: "In particular, Tim incorrectly informed the William Fall Group appraiser during the appraisal process that the Holloway Property had a new roof." Id. The Court found that "[i]n his deposition, Tim backtracked with respect to the newness of the roof, instead testifying that only some of the roof was recently renovated." Id.
Based on the above, the Court held as follows:
In this court's opinion, the foregoing evidence is sufficient to establish a question of fact as to whether Tim breached his duty of good faith by taking opportunistic advantage of the William Fall Group appraisal in a way that could not have been contemplated at the time of the [real estate purchase agreement's] drafting and which, therefore, was not resolved explicitly by the parties.
Jan. 2021 Op. at 9. Thus, the Court denied Tim's motion for summary judgment as to Terry and Yoder Machinery's claims for specific performance of the real estate purchase agreement and for
3

breach of that agreement. Id. The Court also denied Tim summary judgment on his counterclaims for unpaid rent, eviction, and unjust enrichment. Id. at 10.
This Court later granted Terry and Yoder Machinery's request to allow their unjust-enrich- ment claim to proceed, in addition to their other claims. Opinion and Judgment Entry, Terral Yoder, et al. v. Timothy Yoder, No. G-4801-CI-0201904611-000 (Apr. 29, 2021), at 5, 8. This Court also denied Tim's motion for reconsideration of the Court's January 2021 decision. Id. at 8.
In June 2021, the case settled. See Ex. A to Yoder Brothers Defs.' Answer. The settlement agreement resolved the brothers' dispute over the price Tim would be paid for his 50% interest in the real property. The settlement agreement is "by and between TERRAL YODER as Purchaser and TIMOTHY YODER as Seller." Id. Its recital states:
WHEREAS, the parties are in litigation over the sale of a building that they mutu- ally own at 1500 Holloway Road, Holland, Ohio, and a dispute has arisen as to the purchase price and rentals due under the Real Estate Purchase Agreement, along with possible set offs of a Stock Purchase Agreement, that are claims against Tim- othy Yoder, and the parties desire to reduce their agreement to writing.
Id. In the settlement agreement, Terry and Tim agreed (among other things) that (1) Terry would pay Tim over $1.6 million by June 30, 2021; (2) Tim would "sign all documents required under the Real Estate Purchase Agreement to transfer his 50% ownership interest in 1500 Holloway Road to Terral Yoder"; (3) the real-estate lawsuit would be dismissed with prejudice, at each parties' cost; and (4) each party would pay half the mediation bill. Id. The settlement agreement also in- cluded a "Release of Claims" that states:
All claims set forth in the lawsuit, or that could be filed against each party by the other, are hereby settled and dismissed with prejudice. The parties hereby release each other, their heirs, successor and assigns, from all claims that currently exist or that could exist through the present date, known or unknown, claimed or unclaimed. This Release is not effective until the payment is made in Paragraph 1.
Id.
4

II. In June 2024, Yoder Machinery Filed This Lawsuit Against Yoder Brothers Machinery Ltd., Tim Yoder, Ryan Yoder, and Kory Yoder for Spying on Yoder Machinery's Highly Confidential and Proprietary Information.
When Tim left the family business in January 2019, he and his sons Ryan and Kory started a competing company, confusingly called "Yoder Brothers Machinery Ltd." Compl. 111-2, 18- 21. Yoder Machinery's bank, Waterford Bank, was well aware of the contentious dynamic be- tween the competitors. Id. [3. But the Bank took Yoder Brothers Machinery Ltd. on as a customer anyway. Id. At the time of the Yoder Brothers Defendants' exit, Terry specifically instructed the Bank to take Tim, Ryan, and Kory off all Yoder Machinery accounts and to ensure that their email addresses were no longer associated with any Yoder Machinery account or wire. Id. 135. The Bank represented this was done. Id. It was not. Instead, for almost a year and a half, the Bank provided Yoder Brothers Machinery Ltd. with Yoder Machinery's highly confidential and proprietary in- formation, including its customer, pricing, and revenue information. Id. 14. The Yoder Brothers Defendants could have put a stop to this at any time, but they did not-choosing instead to spy on Yoder Machinery to their competitive advantage. Id. 15. The unlawfully disclosed sales infor- mation told the Yoder Brothers Defendants (among other things) (1) who were active buyers in the market, (2) the pricing level of their recent activity, and (3) where to find them. Id. 154. Tim Yoder admitted to reviewing this unlawfully disclosed information. Id. 156.
Seeking to remedy this wrong, Yoder Machinery-the sole plaintiff here-filed this law- suit against the Yoder Brothers Defendants for spying on its highly confidential and proprietary information. Compl. 114-5. Yoder Machinery is also suing Waterford Bank for unlawfully dis- closing that information for almost a year and a half. Yoder Machinery brings a claim against all defendants for misappropriation of trade secrets, in addition to other claims. Id. 1175-85.
5

LAW AND ARGUMENT
I. Terry and Tim's Unambiguous Settlement Agreement Shows that Plaintiff Yoder Machinery Is Not a Party to the Agreement.
A. The plain language and signature blocks establish that Plaintiff is not a party to the agreement.
Terry and Tim's settlement agreement unambiguously establishes that Plaintiff Yoder Ma- chinery is not a party to the agreement. That's what it says, and that's the way it's signed. Defend- ants correctly acknowledge that "[i]f the language of the contract is clear and unambiguous, a Court may not resort to construction of that language." Defs.' Mot. at 9 (citing Hybud Equip. Corp. v. Sphere Drake Ins. Co., 64 Ohio St.3d 657 (1992)). But they only pay lip service to this governing standard and ignore the plain language of the agreement. The one-page agreement (attached as Exhibit A to Defs.' Answer) makes clear who the parties are, and Yoder Machinery is not one of them. The first sentence states that it is "by and between TERRAL YODER as Purchaser and TIMOTHY YODER as Seller." And the agreement nowhere mentions Yoder Machinery. "Terral Yoder" and "Timothy Yoder" are the only parties mentioned in the entire agreement.
Settlement agreements are binding "only upon [parties to the agreement] and not upon a third person." State ex rel. Dillard Dept. Stores v. Ryan, 122 Ohio St.3d 241, 2009-Ohio-2683, 118 (quotations omitted) (holding that settlement agreement between two parties could not bind a dif- ferent entity that was not a party to the agreement). Terry and Tim's settlement agreement does not bind Plaintiff Yoder Machinery.
The Court could stop there. But other plain language also demonstrates that Yoder Ma- chinery is not a party to the agreement. The agreement speaks consistently of two parties, not three. In the settlement-amount section, "Terral Yoder" (not Yoder Machinery) "agrees to pay $1,665,000.00 to Timothy Yoder." Similarly, the transfer-of-real-estate section states that
6

"Timothy Yoder" will "transfer his 50% ownership interest in 1500 Holloway Road to Terral Yoder" (emphasis added). The recital states that the parties "mutually" own the real estate that Terral is purchasing. In addition, the release-of-claims section states that "[a]ll claims set forth in the lawsuit, or that could be filed against each party by the other, are hereby settled .... " (emphasis added). And section 4 provides that "[e]ach party shall pay 1/2 of the mediation bill .... " Again, that makes sense because there are two parties, not three.
The parties' signature blocks also establish that Yoder Machinery was not a party to the agreement. There is no signature block for Yoder Machinery, and Terry did not sign on its behalf. Below are the only signatures on the agreement:
TERRAL YODER
TIMOTHY YOUER
Based on these signature blocks, Terry and Tim signed in their individual, not corporate capacities. The caselaw bears this out across a variety of commercial contexts. For Terry to have signed in a representative capacity on behalf of Yoder Machinery, he would have had to, "in the corporation name, and underneath the corporate name ... sign[ed] his own name, affixing thereto his appropriate official title as an officer of said corporation[.]" See Aungst v. Creque, 72 Ohio St. 551, 554 (1905) (discussing signatures on promissory notes); cf. R.C. 1303.42(B)(2) (negotiable- instruments statute providing that, generally, "if the form of the signature does not show unambig- uously that the signature is made in a representative capacity," then "the representative is liable on the instrument"); Kellam v. Berkshire-Hudson Cap. XI, L.L.C., 2006 WL 2403417, at *5 (E.D. Va.
7

Aug. 18, 2006) (it was clear an individual signed in a corporate capacity where he "sign[ed] under the signature block designated to the contracting corporate entity" and signed his name using his corporate title, "Gary J. Davies, Manager"); Crowder v. Ann L. Crowder Est. Tr., 2007 WL 2874818, at *2 (Tex. App. Oct. 4, 2007) (individual signed settlement agreement in both individual and representative capacities where the signature block identified him as "Walter F. Crowder, In- dividually and as Trustee of the Ann L. Crowder Estate Trust").
Simply put, if Yoder Machinery had been a party to the settlement agreement, and if Terry had signed as its representative on its behalf, the signature block would have been (or a close variation of):
YODER MACHINERY SALES CO. By: Terral Yoder, President
This is standard practice. For example:
ALLIANCE LIFE USA, INC. DBA NATIONAL AGENTS ALLIANCE 1214 Turrentine Street Burlington, NC 28215 By: Andy S. Albright Andy S. Albright, CEO
Cool Springs Fin. Grp., LLC v. Albright, 2024 WL 1144225, at *21 (M.D. Tenn. Mar. 15, 2024). The above signature block, unlike Terry's signature on the settlement agreement, shows the indi- vidual was signing in a corporate capacity: "By signing as 'CEO' on a signature line that starts with 'By' below the name of the company, Albright clearly signaled an intent to sign the NDA in his representative capacity on behalf of ALU and not in his individual capacity." Id. at *23.
Here, not only is Yoder Machinery's name nowhere mentioned, but Terry's representative title ("President") is nowhere mentioned either. Terry does not sign "on a signature line that starts with 'By," he does not sign "underneath the corporate name," and he does not list "his appropriate official title as an officer of said corporation." See Cool Springs Fin. Grp., 2024 WL 1144225, at
8

*23; Aungst, 72 Ohio St. at 554. The signature blocks plainly demonstrate that Terry signed the agreement in an individual capacity only, not in a representative capacity on behalf of Yoder Ma- chinery. This is all the more true where, at the outset of the agreement, the parties made clear it was by and between two individuals.
In interpreting settlement agreements,"[a]s with any other kind of contract, courts presume that the intent of the contracting parties resides in the language they choose to employ in the agree- ment." Alotech Ltd. L.L.C. v. Barnes, 2017-Ohio-5569, 111 (8th Dist.) (citing Shifrin v. Forest City Ents., Inc., 64 Ohio St.3d 635, 638 (1992)). So also here. Terry and Tim's settlement agree- ment does not bind Yoder Machinery, the sole plaintiff here, because Yoder Machinery was not a party to the agreement under its unambiguous terms. And non-parties to settlement agreements are not bound by them. Dillard Dept. Stores, 122 Ohio St.3d 241 at 118.
B. Defendants' contrary contentions do not hold water.
The Yoder Brothers Defendants' cited caselaw says nothing to the contrary. Defendants rest their hopes on Smith v. Buckeye Union Insurance Co., 1980 WL 351507 (6th Dist. Sept. 5, 1980). But Smith is easily distinguishable and of dubious precedential value.
To be sure, Defendants claim that Smith is "controlling Sixth District precedent." Defs.' Mot. at 12. But Smith is an unpublished "decision & journal entry" from 1980 and, therefore, not binding precedent. See State ex rel. Green Tokai, Co. v. Indus. Comm., 2007-Ohio-4688, 17 (10th Dist.) (determining that relator's reliance upon "memorandum decisions" was "unconvincing" be- cause such decisions "have no binding precedential value"). Under the Supreme Court Rules for the Reporting of Opinions, "All opinions of the courts of appeals issued after May 1, 2002 may be cited as legal authority and weighted as deemed appropriate by the courts without regard to whether the opinion was published or in what form it was published." Rep. Op. R. 3.4 ("Use of
9

. Opinions") (emphasis added). Smith falls (well) outside of this rule, is of dubious precedential value, and is not binding.
Smith is also easily distinguishable. Indeed, it fits Plaintiff's plain-language argument, not Defendants' atextual theory. Smith is a medical-malpractice case where the lead plaintiff, Brant Smith, suffered injuries in a car wreck and subsequently alleged a claim for medical malpractice against a doctor and his medical-services company. Id. at *1. He also negotiated a settlement with another plaintiff and the at-fault driver's insurance company. Id. The parties discussed "payment of medical bills and other matters," and after this discussion, the plaintiffs signed a release in exchange for thousands of dollars from the insurance company. Id. Smith signed this release de- spite being "aware of the nature and extent of [his] malpractice claim." Id. at *2. The agreement he signed released not only the insurance company but also "all other persons" from any claims "arising out of" the auto accident. Id. at *1.
The following year, Smith sued the insurance company to have the release set aside, and sued the doctor and his medical-services company for medical malpractice. Smith, 1980 WL 351507, at *2. The court held that the parties' agreement released the medical-malpractice defend- ants as well as the insurance company because "all injuries were known prior to the signing of the release" and because there had been a prior "final judicial determination that the written release is valid and binding on all parties affected." Id. at *3.
Smith does not support the Yoder Brothers Defendants' theory. In Smith-unlike here- the plaintiff was a party to the settlement agreement that released all persons from his claims. Smith, 1980 WL 351507, at *1. Here, Yoder Machinery (the sole plaintiff in this lawsuit) was not a party to the settlement agreement. And settlement agreements, like contracts generally, are bind- ing "only upon such parties" as are "parties to the contract." Dillard Dept. Stores, 122 Ohio St.3d
10

241 at 118 (quotations omitted). Smith is inapt for that simple reason. While the plaintiff in Smith could release even unnamed future defendants from his own known claims, he could not release those defendants from any claims non-signatories might have. If Jane Doe wrecks her car, receives treatment from the same doctor who treated the plaintiff in Smith, and files a medical-malpractice claim, the doctor could not use Smith's release of claims to escape liability as to Jane Doe. A party to a settlement agreement cannot grant immunity to defendants on behalf of all other people for all other conduct. In the same way, Terry could not release any claims that Yoder Machinery might have-because Yoder Machinery was not a party to the settlement agreement.
Smith is inapt for other reasons too. In Smith, the plaintiff was "aware of the nature and extent of [his] malpractice claim" at the time he signed the release. 1980 WL 351507 at *2; see also id. at *3. Here, while Plaintiff discovered Waterford Bank's unlawful disclosure of confiden- tial sales information in 2020, Plaintiff cannot know the "extent of" its injuries until the Yoder Brothers Defendants produce-in discovery-documents sufficient to show the extent to which they benefited from their competitor's trade secrets over a year and a half. See, e.g., Compl. 1159, 79-80, 84. Moreover, in the previous lawsuit against Waterford Bank, voluntarily dismissed with- out prejudice in 2023, Tim Yoder denied Plaintiff critical information regarding the extent of the harm Plaintiff suffered, which Plaintiff reasonably sought through a third-party subpoena for doc- uments. See Ex. 1 to Non-Party Tim Yoder's Motion to Quash Subpoena, Yoder Machinery Sales Co. v. Waterford Bank, No. CI Account (Lucas Cty. Ct. C.P. Aug. 15, 2023).1 This history, .
1 Defendants note (at 2) that the Court granted Tim's motion to quash. However, the motion to quash was unopposed, likely because Plaintiff's counsel withdrew from the case around the same time the motion to quash was filed, and Plaintiff had only recently retained new counsel by the time the Court ruled on the pending motion. See Order, Yoder Machinery Sales Co. v. Waterford Bank, No. CI Account (Lucas Cty. Ct. C.P. Sept. 12, 2023). And the Court specifically granted Yoder Machinery leave to reissue the subpoena. Id.
11
.

combined with Tim Yoder's previous conduct (see above at 2-4), undermines Defendants' melo- dramatic claim that this lawsuit is "abusive and wasteful." Defs.' Mot. at 7. Nor does Plaintiff seek to wage "permanent litigation against the Defendants." Id. at 12. Plaintiff simply seeks to remedy a wrong, the extent of which cannot be known prior to discovery.2
In any event, it would be improper to hold on a motion for judgment on the pleadings (where all material allegations must be construed in the plaintiff's favor) that Yoder Machinery knew the "extent of" its trade-secrets-related injuries when Terry and Tim signed the settlement agreement. See Smith, 1980 WL 351507, at *2. Put another way, whether Yoder Machinery knew the extent of its trade-secrets-related injuries on June 7, 2021 (it did not) is a question of material fact that cannot be resolved on a Rule 12(C) motion. See State ex rel. Leneghan v. Husted, 154 Ohio St. 3d 60, 2018-Ohio-3361, 113 (Rule 12(C) motions may be granted only where "no material factual issues exist" and where "the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law" (quotations omitted)). Regardless, as discussed above, Terry and Tim's settlement agreement does not bind Yoder Machinery because it is not a party to the agreement. See Dillard Dept. Stores, 122 Ohio St.3d 241 at [18.
A final point. The Yoder Brothers Defendants do not make a res judicata argument, so they have waived and/or forfeited any such argument. See State v. Belville, 171 Ohio St.3d 5, 2022- Ohio-3879, 117 n.1. And principles of res judicata further underscore why Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings is improper. Claim preclusion simply "prevents subsequent actions, by
2 Contrary to Defendants' assertion (at 7 n.2), Plaintiff is also not leveling ad hominem attacks at the Yoder Brothers Defendants. The allegations in paragraph 32 of the Complaint directly relate to Waterford Bank's meeting the standard for actual malice under Ohio law by underscoring Wa- terford Bank's (at best) reckless disregard of the risk to Plaintiff and Plaintiff's rights and interests by failing to check to make sure that the Yoder Brothers Defendants were actually removed from Plaintiff's accounts and wires. That is obvious from the flow of the Complaint, including the very next paragraph. See Compl. 133; see also Compl. 1169, 33-68. -
12

the same parties or their privies, based upon any claim arising out of a transaction that was the subject matter of a previous action." O'Nesti v. DeBartolo Realty Corp., 113 Ohio St. 3d 59, 2007- Ohio-1102, 16 (emphasis added).
Here, determining whether all the parties are in privity with one another would require extrinsic evidence, which must not be considered in ruling on a Rule 12(C) motion. See O'Nesti, 113 Ohio St. 3d 59 at 125. And fundamentally, this lawsuit based on the Yoder Brothers Defend- ants' subsequent competitive spying on the Company does not "aris[e] out of a transaction that was the subject matter of" the previous dispute. Id. at 16; cf. Grava v. Parkman Twp., 73 Ohio St. 3d 379, 383 (1995) (res judicata applied where, "[i]n both instances, [the party] was attempting to construct exactly the same building on the same tract of land"). The previous litigation was over an actual "transaction" involving a real estate purchase agreement and the amount of money Tim would be paid based on competing valuations of the Holloway Property. The present lawsuit is about the Yoder Brothers Defendants' subsequent competitive spying. And of course, "res judicata is not a shield to protect the blameworthy." Davis v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 93 Ohio St. 3d 488, 491 (2001).3
3 More fully explained, the previous lawsuit was a lawsuit about an actual, discrete, M&A transaction. The suit was specifically about completing that M&A transaction and how much money the former business partner (used only in the colloquial sense) would make in the transac- tion. This suit is about a competitor's subsequent spying on Yoder Machinery and about Waterford Bank's liability for its involvement in the same. The fact that Tim displayed a consciousness of guilt in that corporate spying by, when discovered, immediately retaliating against Terry through an eviction notice, does not make this lawsuit for subsequent spying arise out of the prior M&A transaction, in a res judicata sense, any more than it makes Yoder Machinery subject to the terms of a settlement agreement where it is not a party to that agreement. Contra Defs.' Mot. at 5. And it makes sense why Terry and Tim were the only parties to the settlement agreement. They owned the real estate individually, and the gravamen of the suit for completing the M&A transaction was the real estate. Put simply, if the parties in the M&A suit wanted to agree to give Tim, his sons, and their subsequent business entity blanket immunity for the corporate spying that occurred after the M&A transaction-where Yoder Machinery had not, and could not have, determined the extent
13

II. Any Other Argument Requires Extrinsic Evidence, Which Must Not Be Considered in Ruling on the Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings. .
The unambiguous language shows that the settlement agreement is between only Terry and Tim Yoder in their individual capacities, and that Yoder Machinery is not a party. Defendants do not argue that the settlement agreement is ambiguous, so they have waived and/or forfeited any such argument. See Belville, 171 Ohio St.3d 5 at 117 n.1.
Regardless, even if Defendants could establish that the settlement agreement is ambiguous, that would simply confirm that their motion is improper. A Rule 12(C) determination is "restricted solely to the allegations of the pleadings," State ex rel. Pirman v. Money, 69 Ohio St. 3d 591, 593 (1994), and thus cannot consider extrinsic or parol evidence. See Leneghan, 154 Ohio St. 3d 60 at 117 (denying Rule 12(C) motion and holding that because "a motion for judgment on the pleadings tests the allegations of the complaint and therefore presents a pure question of law," a party's submitted "affidavit is therefore not a proper basis upon which to grant judgment on the plead- ings"). And any evidence Defendants might try to put on would most certainly be disputed. For example, Tim might testify that he understood the settlement agreement to bind Yoder Machinery, while Terry might testify that he was signing in an individual capacity only. Resolving that dispute would be a matter of weighing the evidence and making credibility determinations-far outside the scope of a Rule 12(C) motion. See Pirman, 69 Ohio St. 3d at 593; Leneghan, 154 Ohio St. 3d 60 at 117.
This raises a final issue. Defendants request that the Court, pursuant to Evidence Rule 201, take judicial notice of the parties' voluntary dismissal of the real-estate lawsuit. See Defs.' Mot. at 6 n.1. To be sure, it may be appropriate for a court to "take notice of a fact (e.g., that certain
of the transgression committed against it or the corresponding harms-then they would have said so and made Plaintiff a party to the agreement. But they didn't.
14
.

documents were filed)." State ex rel. Mather v. Oda, 174 Ohio St. 3d 526, 2023-Ohio-3907, 114. But a court may not "accept the documents themselves as evidence" because "[t]he admission of documents into evidence is outside the scope of Evid.R. 201." Id.
In any event, Defendants may not use the voluntary dismissal to contend that Yoder Ma- chinery must be a party to the settlement agreement because it was a party in the lawsuit that was voluntarily dismissed. That contention improperly uses the voluntary dismissal as extrinsic, parol evidence of what the parties must have meant when they settled the real-estate dispute. There are two key problems with that: (1) Defendants have not established (or even argued) that the settle- ment agreement is ambiguous, so they cannot introduce parol evidence; and (2) they cannot intro- duce parol evidence on a Rule 12(C) motion anyway. (For the same reason, even if the Court found the settlement agreement to be ambiguous, that would simply confirm that Defendants' motion must be denied.) But the Court need not reach this extrinsic-evidence analysis because Defendants have not argued that the settlement agreement is ambiguous. And on that point, the parties agree: Terry and Tim's settlement agreement is unambiguous. As discussed above, the agreement plainly shows that Yoder Machinery is not a party to it, and thus, not bound by it. See Dillard Dept. Stores, 122 Ohio St.3d 241 at 118.
CONCLUSION
For all these reasons, the Court should deny the Yoder Brothers Defendants' motion for partial judgment on the pleadings.
Respectfully submitted, /s/ Joseph P. Ashbrook Joseph P. Ashbrook (0091279) Benjamin M. Flowers (0095284) Andrew D. McCartney (0099853) Ashbrook Byrne Kresge LLC
